claims.wording: No one counted the silver at the time. The figures come from merchants and missionaries, most of them far from the ship. Kobata, the Japanese historian of the mines, wrote that Japan's output in these years cannot now be calculated. Kobata, Atwell and von Glahn all quote Fitch's figure. A later historian, Kent Deng, warns that European traders almost certainly mixed Japanese silver with silver from elsewhere, so the same silver can be counted twice.
claims.notes:
Quote: "it is now impossible to calculate the production of gold and silver in Japan" (Kobata, p. 247); "based principally on statements of contemporary European merchants and missionaries" (von Glahn, p. 133); "European traders (mainly the Portuguese and the Dutch) almost certainly mixed Japanese silver with silver from other parts of the world for payment."; "There is a real danger of double counting." (Deng, p. 326); "every year the silver amounted to more than 600,000 cruzados" (Kobata, p. 253); "above six hundred thousand cruzados" (Atwell 1982, p. 71); "about six hundred thousand cruzados" (von Glahn, p. 129)

confidence.rationale: high that the Sources say no count exists and that modern totals differ. No number is given here.

claims.wording: Souza estimates that Portuguese ships took 7.5 to 8.9 million taels of silver out of Japan between 1580 and 1597. He reached it by taking Kobata's estimate of 500,000 to 600,000 taels a year, about 18,700 to 22,500 kilograms, and multiplying by the years in which a ship sailed. Kobata had reached his from the figures of Fitch and two Jesuits. Souza calls his data far from perfect. Other modern totals are twice as high or more, and von Glahn rejects them.
claims.notes:
